title: Sikh architecture
hook: domes, small pavilions, pools and open doors

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sikh painting, from janamsakhi scenes to Sobha Singh's portraits. Your line was faith in paint. What was the maker of that picture on your wall trying to honor? Day one thousand three hundred forty-nine.

From the street, the first thing you see is the dome: rounded, ribbed like the petals of a closed lotus, with a gilded tip. Along the roofline, small open pavilions with their own little domes, like lanterns set out on a wall. Out front, a tall flagpole wrapped in cloth, a saffron flag at the top. Inside the gate, maybe a pool of still water, reflecting all of it. And the doors. Count them. Today's word is the way Sikhs build: what the shapes are, and what the doors are saying.
screen: `A RIBBED DOME, A GILDED TIP.` → `SMALL PAVILIONS ON THE ROOF.` → `AND THE DOORS.`

segments.voice: First, the shapes. Classic Sikh architecture draws on the building styles of its region and gives them its own accent: the ribbed dome, often called lotus-shaped; the small domed pavilions, called chhatris, lining the roof; arched windows; gilded or white surfaces that catch the light. Outside stands the Nishan Sahib, the flagpole that tells a traveler from far off that a gurdwara is here. Second, the water. Some gurdwaras have a sarovar, a pool, where people may bathe or simply sit and look. The building and its reflection become one picture. Third, the doors. Tradition says the Harmandir in Amritsar was built open on all four sides, and that this is the point: no side is the front door for one kind of person and the back door for another. Whoever comes, from whichever direction, walks straight in. Tradition also says the Harmandir sits lower than the ground around it, so everyone steps down to enter. Fourth, the line behind the doors. In Raag Suhi, Guru Arjan names the four classes of his society, the Kshatriya, the Brahmin, the Shudra and the Vaishya, and says, in paraphrase, that the teaching is shared by all four. Tradition reads the four doors as that line in brick and marble. A building can preach without saying a word: it tells you, before you're even inside, who is welcome. A gurdwara in any style, in any country, is meant to say the same: the door is open, the kitchen is open, and nobody asks who you are. Open on all sides.
screen: `RIBBED DOMES AND SMALL PAVILIONS.` · `A POOL THAT DOUBLES THE PICTURE.` · `DOORS ON ALL FOUR SIDES.` · `THE TEACHING IS SHARED BY ALL FOUR.` · then, large: `OPEN ON ALL SIDES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice a building's doors. Settle, and breathe. Think of a building you go into often: your home, your workplace, a place of worship, a shop. Where are its doors? Which one do guests use, and which one is for some people and not others? Who might feel unwelcome at the door, and why? Don't fix anything yet. Just see the doors clearly. Then picture a building with an open door on every side. The bell holds the time.
Sikh architecture. Ribbed domes, small rooftop pavilions, pools, a flag out front, and doors that say everyone may come in. Today's word.

Your line: open on all sides. Today, notice one door in your life, a real one or a social one, that's open to some people and not others, and hold it open for someone. Day one thousand three hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Gurdwaras are built in different styles, from classic domed buildings with chhatris and a sarovar to converted local buildings; each flies the Nishan Sahib and keeps its doors and langar open to all.
